                                   PROJECT NO. 58000

RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                          §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                      §
TRANSMISSION COST                             §                  OF TEXAS
RECOVERY IN THE ERCOT                         §
REGION                                        §



                   COMMENTS OF AMERICAN BITCOIN CORP.

I.     INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
American Bitcoin Corp. ("ABTC") respectfully submits these comments on the Proposal
for Publication ("PFP") approved at the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s
(“Commission”) July 9, 2026 open meeting on Project No. 58000. ABTC is an industrial-
scale Bitcoin mining company with demonstrated operating and payment history across
multiple large, flexible load sites in ERCOT.
ABTC supports the principle that large loads should pay the costs they cause and that
speculative interconnection reservations should not strand costs on other customers. To
that end, ABTC raises three concerns below, responds to the Commission Staff’s
questions, and joins other commenters in urging coordination with Project No. 58481,
including express confirmation in §25.192(k) that amounts already paid or secured under
§25.194 are not recovered a second time through rates.
II.    ABTC’S THREE CORE RECOMMENDATIONS
ABTC raises three concerns with the PFP and recommends the following:
1.     Apply the Minimum Billing Demand Prospectively
ABTC’s position is that the minimum billing demand should apply only to new and
expanded interconnections, not to existing energized capacity that has already
demonstrated it pays. Senate Bill 6 states that large load interconnection standards “must
apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded interconnection.” The PFP follows
that structure: the minimum applies to a “large load customer” defined as an entity
subject to §25.194, which implements PURA §37.0561 for new and expanded
interconnections. ABTC urges the Commission to confirm this scope expressly in the rule
text.
The policy rationale supports this reading. The minimum targets speculative reservations
that fail to materialize. An operating, energized facility is the opposite case: built, paying,
and posing no stranded-cost risk. Two clarifications would make the prospective scope
administrable: (1) an increase in measured non-coincident peak (“NCP”) demand within


                                              1
 existing contracted capacity is an operating observation, not an interconnection request,
and should not trigger the minimum; and (2) where an existing site expands, the
minimum should apply only to the incremental capacity added, not the full facility.
2. Preserve Flexible Loads’ Incentive to Curtail
ABTC’s position is that a minimum billing demand set at contracted or NCP peak
eliminates the economic incentive for flexible loads to curtail, and that ERCOT’s
reliability and cost outcomes depend in part on preserving that curtailment capacity.
Bitcoin mining is the most interruptible large load class in ERCOT. The Independent
Market Monitor has reported that cryptocurrency mining accounted for more than half of
all Emergency Response Service capacity by end of 2025; EIA has documented that these
loads routinely curtail in response to high prices and scarcity. That behavior lowers
realized peaks, defers transmission investment, and caps scarcity-price events for all
customers.
Making transmission charges invariant to curtailment removes the reason to curtail.
ABTC’s concern is that this outcome would increase realized peaks, defer the grid
benefits that curtailment currently provides, and risk leaving transmission facilities
without the anchor load that justified their construction — the precise stranded-cost
outcome the rule is designed to prevent. ABTC urges the Commission to ensure the rule
does not produce that result.
ABTC’s recommended fix is not an exemption. ABTC’s position is that flexible loads
should be billed on demand actually placed at peak, and that curtailment should be
recognized only where contractually committed and independently verifiable.
3. Adopt a Seasonal Coincident-Peak Methodology
ABTC’s position is that equal-weighted 12CP does not accurately reflect cost causation
and should be replaced with a seasonal 8CP methodology—or, at minimum, a hybrid
with a material seasonal component.
ABTC recognizes that ERCOT transmission investment reflects locational constraints
and year-round operating conditions as well as system-wide demand. But in ABTC’s
view, equal-weighted 12CP allocates cost without regard to which months actually drive
transmission investment, undermining the cost-causation principles the methodology is
meant to serve. Under 4CP, each selected interval carries 25% of the annual allocator;
under equal-weighted 12CP, that figure drops to 8.33% per interval, which is a material
dilution of the price signal at each critical peak. A seasonal 8CP methodology would
preserve a concentrated response signal during periods of greatest system stress while
recognizing winter risk.




                                           2
 III.   RESPONSES TO THE COMMISSION’S QUESTIONS
Question 1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing
demand be different for customers with different contracted peak demands or
different NCP demands?
ABTC’s position is yes, but the appropriate differentiator is flexibility, not size. Identical
contracted peaks impose very different costs depending on whether a customer curtails at
coincident peaks. ABTC recommends that flexibility be locked in contractually through
Controllable Load Resource registration or an enforceable commitment to curtail to a
specified firm level during peak intervals and emergencies, rather than assumed. A
customer’s minimum billing demand should reflect its committed firm level, not its full
contracted peak.
Question 2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be (a) fixed for 20 years
as proposed, (b) reduced in phases over a period of 20 years, or (c) extended to a
longer time period?
ABTC’s position is option (b) phased reduction, applied prospectively only. As an
energized load pays its charges, the stranded-cost exposure that justifies a high minimum
diminishes; a flat 20-year floor overstates that risk long after it has dissipated. Any
minimum should also be net of CIAC, fees, and security already paid or posted for the
same facilities or risk.
Question 3. Should the large load minimum billing demand instead reflect a
“ratcheted” demand or a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, and should
any such percentage decline in phases over the years?
ABTC supports a ratcheted structure phased down over time, tying billing to
demonstrated demand while preserving early-period cost-recovery. The ratchet should be
anchored to contracted peak demand, not NCP. A customer’s single highest interval,
which may occur off-peak when consumption benefits the system, does not measure
contribution to the coincident peaks that size the network. NCP belongs only on
separately identified local facilities sized to a customer’s maximum demand.
Question 4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational
load (an entity subject to §25.194 in which 50% or greater of site demand consists of
power-electronic-based computational load, such as data centers and
cryptocurrency mining facilities)?
No, ABTC’s position is that a megawatt costs the same to serve regardless of end use,
and rate classifications must rest on cost-of-service distinctions consistent with PURA
§36.003. Computational loads are also far from uniform. Flexibility varies widely among
Bitcoin mining, HPC, and enterprise data centers so an end-use class would overcharge




                                              3
 some and undercharge others. Any differentiation should track verified flexibility; for
Bitcoin mining, that supports lower peak-driven cost per connected megawatt, not higher.
Question 5. Should the definition of transmission interconnection costs be
broadened to include transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a
batch study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?
ABTC’s position is that this definition should not be broadened, or should be broadened
only narrowly. Batch-study upgrades typically benefit the wider system, not just the
triggering customer. Any expansion should be limited to facilities clearly and solely
required by a specific customer’s own interconnection request.
Question 6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity
irrespective of whether it has energized or is fully using available capacity, how
should these loads be reflected in resource adequacy reports, assessments, and
transmission planning studies?
ABTC’s position is that studies should use the milestone-based energization schedules
customers already disclose under §25.194, rather than counting full contracted peak
demand as firm from the date of reservation. Loads with enforceable curtailment
commitments should be reflected at their committed firm level, so that planning does not
overbuild to speculative or curtailable demand.
IV.    CONCLUSION
ABTC respectfully requests that the Commission: (1) confirm that the minimum billing
demand applies prospectively, consistent with PURA §37.0561, and only to incremental
capacity when an existing site expands; (2) preserve the incentive for committed,
verifiable curtailable loads to curtail at peak rather than billing them as if firm; (3) adopt
a seasonal 8CP methodology in lieu of equal-weighted 12CP; and (4) coordinate with
Project No. 58481 to prevent double recovery of amounts already paid or secured under
§25.194.




                                              4
       Respectfully submitted,

      Casey Bell
      State Bar No. 24012271
      BALCH & BINGHAM LLP
      600 Congress Avenue, Suite 2700
      Austin, Texas 78701
      Telephone: (512) 744-9300
      Facsimile: (512) 744-9399
      Email: cabell@balch.com


By:      /s/ Casey Bell
         Casey Bell

      ATTORNEY FOR AMERICAN
      BITCOIN CORP.

                               EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
                       Submitted by: American Bitcoin Corp.


ABTC’s comments        in   Project   No.   58000   make    the   following   substantive
recommendations:
 •   Apply the minimum billing demand prospectively only, consistent with PURA
     §37.0561: exclude existing energized capacity expressly in the rule text; an NCP
     increase within existing contracted capacity should not trigger the minimum;
     expansions should subject only the incremental capacity added.
 •   Preserve flexible loads’ incentive to curtail: bill flexible loads on demand actually
     placed at peak, recognizing curtailment only where contractually committed and
     independently verifiable.
 •   Adopt a seasonal 8CP methodology — or, at minimum, a hybrid with a material
     seasonal component — in lieu of equal-weighted 12CP.
 •   Adopt a phased reduction of the minimum billing demand rather than a flat 20-year
     floor, net of CIAC, fees, and security already paid or posted.
 •   Anchor any ratcheted minimum to contracted peak demand, not NCP demand.
 •   Do not adopt separate end-use rate treatment for large computational loads; any
     differentiation should track verified flexibility, consistent with PURA §36.003.
 •   Do not broaden transmission interconnection costs beyond facilities clearly and
     solely required by a specific customer’s own request; base planning treatment of
     reserved capacity on milestone-based energization schedules.
 •   Coordinate with Project No. 58481 and confirm in §25.192(k) that amounts already
     paid or secured under §25.194 are not recovered a second time through rates.
